In 1690 Job Charnock, an agent of the English East India Company, set up a trading post at Sutanuti on the Hooghly River in Bengal. With the villages of Kalikata and Gobindapur, bought in 1698, it grew into Calcutta, now Kolkata.

The Company wanted a safe base in Bengal, the richest province of the Mughal Empire, famed for its cotton and silk cloth, saltpetre and rice. The site was swampy and unhealthy but easy to defend and reachable by sea ships. The English built Fort William there.

In 1756 the nawab Siraj ud-Daulah took the town. The British took it back and won the Battle of Plassey the next year. From then on Calcutta grew fast. It was the capital of British India from 1772 to 1911, when the capital moved to New Delhi.

It became the home of the Bengal Renaissance, of thinkers such as Ram Mohan Roy and Rabindranath Tagore. Whether Charnock should be called its founder is debated, since people lived in the villages long before him.
